clinicalPearls: Now largely reclassified as autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD), with UMOD and MUC1 the commonest causative genes.
Inheritance is autosomal dominant, with slowly progressive chronic kidney disease and characteristically bland urine showing little or no proteinuria or haematuria.
UMOD (uromodulin) disease typically causes hyperuricaemia and early-onset gout, often preceding renal impairment.
Cysts are few, small and corticomedullary and are frequently absent, so the historical name is a misnomer and the diagnosis is not made on imaging.
Kidneys are normal or small in size and imaging is usually non-specific.
Distinguish it from nephronophthisis, which is autosomal recessive, causes end-stage disease in childhood or adolescence and has retinal, hepatic and skeletal associations.
Diagnosis rests on family history, clinical phenotype and genetic testing; biopsy shows tubulointerstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy.
Management is supportive, progressing over decades to end-stage renal disease requiring renal replacement or transplantation.
reference.pathophysiology: Medullary cystic kidney disease belongs to a group of autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial diseases caused by mutations in genes expressed in the distal nephron. UMOD mutations cause misfolding and intracellular retention of uromodulin within thick ascending limb cells, provoking endoplasmic reticulum stress and tubular injury, whereas MUC1 frameshift mutations generate a toxic mucin-1 neoprotein; HNF1B and REN mutations account for further cases. The common pathway is progressive tubulointerstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy with relatively bland urine, and corticomedullary cysts, when present, are a secondary and inconstant feature.
additionalDifferentials: Familial juvenile hyperuricaemic nephropathy (part of the UMOD spectrum)
Alport syndrome or thin basement membrane disease
additionalInvestigations: Detailed family pedigree and inheritance assessment
Renal ultrasound (normal or small kidneys; cysts inconstant)
Serial renal function and eGFR trajectory
Renal biopsy where genetics are unavailable, showing tubulointerstitial fibrosis
redFlags: Uraemic symptoms indicating advanced chronic kidney disease
Extrarenal features suggesting an alternative genetic syndrome
reference.prognosis: The disease progresses slowly over decades, with most affected individuals reaching end-stage renal disease in adulthood; transplantation is successful because the condition does not recur in the graft.
pitfalls: Expecting imaging cysts to confirm the diagnosis when they are often absent
Confusing autosomal recessive nephronophthisis with autosomal dominant ADTKD
Missing UMOD disease in young patients presenting with gout and chronic kidney disease
Overlooking the family history because of variable expression
references: KDIGO consensus report on autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease
